_note: Plain guidance shown on the body map for each reading: how to take it, why it matters in space, and what to do when it is outside the usual range. General guidance written by the team, not medical advice. Risk names come from NASA's Human Research Program risk list (source hrp_risks).

resting_hr.measure: Sit still for five minutes after waking, before coffee or exercise, and read the chest strap or a pulse check.
resting_hr.why: Without gravity, the heart and blood vessels adapt to a new normal. NASA lists cardiovascular adaptations as a risk of spaceflight.
resting_hr.act: Recheck tomorrow at the same time. If it stays high for several days, rest, drink your planned fluid and tell the Medical Officer.

hrv.measure: Read it from the chest strap during the same five-minute morning rest as your heart rate.
hrv.why: A drop often comes with poor sleep, stress or illness, so it can flag trouble before you feel it.
hrv.act: Prioritise sleep and an easier workload today. Tell the Medical Officer if it stays low with other changes.

bp_sys.measure: Seated, arm resting at heart level, cuff on bare skin. Take two readings a minute apart and log the second.
bp_sys.why: Blood pressure shows how the heart and vessels are adapting, part of NASA's cardiovascular adaptation risk.
bp_sys.act: Recheck after five quiet minutes. Persistent high readings go to the Medical Officer.

bp_dia.measure: Taken with the systolic reading, from the same cuff.
bp_dia.why: Read together with systolic pressure to see how the heart and vessels are adapting.
bp_dia.act: Recheck after rest. Persistent high readings go to the Medical Officer.

ortho_rise.measure: Lie or float still for five minutes, then stand (or load into a harness) and note how much your heart rate rises within ten minutes.
ortho_rise.why: After weeks without gravity, standing up can make the heart race and cause dizziness, which matters most when landing on Mars.
ortho_rise.act: Stand up slowly, drink your planned fluid, and tell the Medical Officer if you feel faint.

spo2.measure: Clip the finger sensor on a warm finger and keep still for 30 seconds.
spo2.why: Low oxygen can come from illness or poor cabin air. NASA lists hypoxia as a spaceflight risk.
spo2.act: Recheck on another finger. If it stays low, check the cabin air reading and tell the Medical Officer straight away.

exercise_min.measure: Logged by the exercise rig, or entered by hand after each session.
exercise_min.why: Without gravity, bones and muscles weaken unless they are loaded every day.
exercise_min.act: Make up missed sessions over the week. Tell the Medical Officer if pain stops you exercising.

exercise_load.measure: Read from the resistive exercise device at the end of each session.
exercise_load.why: Load shows whether muscles and bones are getting enough work, not just time on the rig.
exercise_load.act: Work back up to your prescribed loads over several sessions.

grip.measure: Squeeze the hand dynamometer three times with your dominant hand and log the best.
grip.why: Grip strength is a quick check on overall muscle strength, which NASA tracks under reduced musculoskeletal fitness.
grip.act: Keep up resistive exercise. A steady fall over weeks goes to the Medical Officer.

bone_marker.measure: From a blood or urine sample, analysed on board or sent to Earth.
bone_marker.why: Bone breaks down faster in weightlessness. NASA lists spaceflight-induced bone changes as a risk.
bone_marker.act: Keep up resistive exercise and your planned diet. A falling trend goes to the Medical Officer.

lean_mass.measure: Estimated from body mass and fitness readings.
lean_mass.why: Muscle is lost quickly in microgravity without daily loading.
lean_mass.act: Keep up resistive exercise and eat your full planned meals.

temp.measure: Oral thermometer, same time each morning, before eating or drinking.
temp.why: A rise is often the first sign of infection. NASA lists altered immune responses as a risk.
temp.act: Rest and drink fluids. Recheck in six hours. A temperature that keeps rising goes to the Medical Officer.

crp.measure: From a blood sample on the weekly draw.
crp.why: CRP rises with inflammation and infection, a sign the immune system is busy.
crp.act: Read it with your temperature and symptoms. Rising CRP with other changes goes to the Medical Officer.

il6.measure: From the same weekly blood sample as CRP.
il6.why: IL-6 is a signal immune cells send when fighting something.
il6.act: Read it with CRP and temperature. Tell the Medical Officer if several rise together.

lymph.why: Changes in white blood cells show how the immune system is coping with stress and the closed cabin.
lymph.act: Read it with your other immune readings. Changes that persist go to the Medical Officer.

symptoms.measure: Rate how you feel in the daily check-in: 0 is none, 5 is severe.
symptoms.why: How you feel often changes before the numbers do.
symptoms.act: Any symptom of 3 or more, or one that is new, goes to the Medical Officer.

sleep_hours.measure: From the sleep band, or your own estimate in the morning.
sleep_hours.why: Crews often sleep less than planned. NASA lists inadequate sleep and irregular schedules as a risk.
sleep_hours.act: Protect your sleep window: dim lights, quiet, and no screens in your sleep station. Tell the Medical Officer if it stays short.

sleep_eff.measure: From the sleep band: time asleep divided by time in bed.
sleep_eff.why: Broken sleep is less restful even when the hours look fine.
sleep_eff.act: Keep the same bedtime each day. Mention it at the next crew health check.

mood.measure: Rate it in the daily check-in from 1 to 10.
mood.why: Isolation and confinement affect mood. NASA lists behavioral changes as a risk.
mood.act: Talk to someone you trust, on board or at home. A low stretch goes to the Medical Officer.

stress.measure: Rate it in the daily check-in from 1 to 10.
stress.why: Long missions bring constant workload and little privacy.
stress.act: Take a short break and try the breathing exercise. Persistent high stress goes to the Medical Officer.

energy.measure: Rate it in the daily check-in from 1 to 10.
energy.why: Low energy can come from poor sleep, illness or low mood.
energy.act: Check your sleep and meals. Mention a long low stretch to the Medical Officer.

social_min.measure: Minutes spent with crewmates or calling home, logged in the check-in.
social_min.why: Crews in long isolation studies became less active and more withdrawn over time.
social_min.act: Plan a shared meal or a call home.

journal.measure: Optional journal in the check-in. Only a tone score is kept unless you choose to keep the words.
journal.why: Tone can show a slide in mood before you notice it yourself.
journal.act: Nothing to do. It feeds the behavior picture.

glucose.measure: Finger-stick meter before breakfast, after at least eight hours without food.
glucose.why: Eating and activity change in flight. NASA lists inadequate food and nutrition as a risk, and the CSA notes that weightlessness resembles a sedentary lifestyle.
glucose.act: Below 70 mg/dL is low: treat it as your medical kit says and tell the Medical Officer. 100 or above on a fasting check: recheck next week and mention it at the crew health check.

body_mass.measure: Weekly, at the same time of day, on the body mass device.
body_mass.why: Body mass shows whether you are eating enough for your workload. NASA lists inadequate food and nutrition as a risk.
body_mass.act: Eat your full planned meals. Steady loss goes to the Medical Officer.

co2.measure: Read the cabin air monitor in your work area.
co2.why: In a closed cabin, carbon dioxide builds up if scrubbers or air flow fail. NASA limits it to a one-hour average of 3 mmHg, and crews have reported headaches between 2.8 and 4.5 mmHg.
co2.act: Above 3 mmHg: check the scrubber and air flow, move to a better ventilated module, and tell the Commander.

fiber.measure: Count servings of fiber-rich food in the daily check-in.
fiber.why: A varied diet supports the gut and overall nutrition on long missions.
fiber.act: Aim for some fiber at most meals. It builds Gut City.

processed.measure: Count servings of processed food in the daily check-in.
processed.why: Long missions rely on stored food, so balance matters.
processed.act: Balance processed meals with fresher options where you can.

daily_dose.measure: Read your personal dosimeter at the end of each day.
daily_dose.why: Space radiation is invisible. NASA lists radiation-induced cancer as a risk and sets career and per-storm limits.
daily_dose.act: If a solar storm warning comes, follow the shelter steps on the Radiation screen.
